skills.name: Word class depends on the sentence
skills.description: Nouns and verbs that share a spelling.

ENG_ADJ_ADV_MIX.label: Mixes up adjectives and adverbs
ENG_ADJ_ADV_MIX.explanation: Calls 'quietly' an adjective, or every -ly word an adverb.

ENG_FIXED_WORD_CLASS.label: Thinks a word always has the same word class
ENG_FIXED_WORD_CLASS.explanation: Calls 'run' a verb even in 'we went for a run'.

questions.prompt: In the sentence "The tortoise moved slowly across the road.", what part of speech is "slowly"?
hints: An adjective describes a noun (a quiet library). An adverb describes a verb (closed quietly).
Not every -ly word is an adverb: lovely and friendly describe nouns.
solution: "slowly" describes how something is done (a verb).
So it is an adverb.

questions.prompt: In the sentence "We went for a run before school.", what part of speech is "run"?
hints: Look at what the word is doing in THIS sentence.
After 'a', 'the' or 'my' it is usually a noun; if it's the action, it's a verb.
solution: Here "run" is a thing (it comes after a/the).
So it is a noun in this sentence.

adjectives_and_adverbs.title: Adjectives and adverbs
adjectives_and_adverbs.big_idea: Adjectives describe nouns (a quiet library). Adverbs describe verbs: how, when or where something happens (closed the door quietly). The -ly ending is a clue, not a rule: lovely and friendly are adjectives.
steps: Find the word it is describing.
If it describes a person, place or thing, it's an adjective.
If it describes an action (how, when, where), it's an adverb.
After verbs like is, looks, smells, feels, a describing word is usually an adjective (the soup smells delicious).
adjectives_and_adverbs.sense_check: Try 'a lovely ___': a lovely painting works, so 'lovely' describes a noun.

worked_examples.prompt: "He closed the door quietly." What is "quietly"?
steps: It tells us HOW he closed the door.

worked_examples.prompt: "Her lovely painting won a prize." What is "lovely"?
steps: Even though it ends in -ly, it's an adjective.

word_class_in_context.title: Word class depends on the sentence
word_class_in_context.big_idea: Many words can be a noun in one sentence and a verb in another. You can only tell by looking at the job the word does in that sentence.
steps: Is the word a thing (often after a, the, my)? Then it's a noun.
Is it the action someone does? Then it's a verb.
Don't decide from the word alone.
word_class_in_context.sense_check: 'I run' (verb) and 'a run' (noun): same word, different jobs.

worked_examples.prompt: "We went for a run." What is "run"?
steps: It names a thing we went for.
It's what we are asked to do.
